extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing newspaper sports stories (match reports, previews, reviews, race accounts, billiards, boxing) and local society items, including what facts to include, appropriate tone, and reporting logistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tennis match reporting — descriptive play and statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the contest with detailed account of strokes, rallies, net play, placement and movement; include point-by-point or set statistics (nets, outs, aces, places) and tables showing points/games per set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vivid description of strokes and tactics (forehand, cross volleys, net approaches), compare players' styles and powers, note who controlled rallies and why; include statistical tallies (e.g., nets and outs totals, aces, places, points by set) to explain differences in outcome. Example in text: detailed narrative of Johnston vs. McLoughlin with a First Set/Second Set points/games table and counts of nets/outs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boxing match structure — general account plus round-by-round detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Write boxing stories as a combination: first a full general account (fighters, character of boxing, weights, heights, reach, methods, crowd, receipts, exact times), then a detailed running story of the fight by rounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first part should cover who the fighters are, physical stats, financials and atmosphere; the second part should be a round-by-round narrative describing key blows, clinches, and momentum shifts. The Willard–Moran match is given as a model illustrating both parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensationalism in boxing reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Present the wholesome rather than the unwholesome side of boxing; avoid appealing to readers' barbaric instincts or reveling in blood and gore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose details that emphasize skill, dexterity and generalship rather than graphic depictions of injury. The text contrasts wholesome coverage with examples that 'savor rather of the Spanish bull-ring' and urges reporters to avoid feeding 'lust for battle.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Automobile race reporting — results, lap-by-lap, incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a clear results summary (driver, time, average) and a lap-by-lap account; report mechanical troubles, changes in lead, starting/trial lap procedures and crowd reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide finishing times and averages (e.g., 'Resta 58:54 102.85'), narrate key moments (tire trouble, stops, pit changes), note starting order and officials (flagman), and describe how the race developed over laps with specific lap descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Billiards reporting — record individual runs and averages
rubrics_metrics.description: When covering billiard matches, emphasize the scoring of individual runs and players' averages; if writing innings/innings-by-innings, follow the same running style as in golf and racing stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report high runs, averages (given as fractional averages in text), and provide explicit inning/run listings when necessary (example: Hoppe—49, 30, 2, ... —500. Average, 19 6-26).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtaining information and press logistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Secure press tickets and press-box seating; use telegraph and telephone wires or arrange messengers to transmit bulletins; take notes to allow very fast dispatch of bulletins during contests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press seats/press-box often have wires; if not installed, have the local telegraph company provide at least two messengers to take bulletins; notes should be taken so bulletins can be given within seconds for quarter/half/inning reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of personal opinion — recognize hybrid story types
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain sporting stories (advance pieces, after-event reviews, and general sport pieces) are hybrids between news and editorial: they may present facts and also interpret or argue a viewpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that combining presentation and interpretation changes the story's purpose; when inserting opinion (e.g., asserting a team 'has a chance'), make clear the interpretive element and avoid disguising opinion as pure news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance (preliminary) stories — include predictions and practical details
rubrics_metrics.description: Advance writeups should include predictions of outcome, effect on future events, player and official names, absences of important men, opinions from coaches/trainers/followers, weaknesses, local/national interest, time/place, and directions/logistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such pieces require reporters who can observe and analyze to give reasonable predictions; include practical information (routes to grounds, seating directions) and human-interest details to engage readers. Example: 'PROMINENT OFFICIALS AT GAME TO-DAY' with teams, place, time, routes and probable line-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review/analytical stories — explain why results occurred
rubrics_metrics.description: Review pieces written after a game should analyze play and explain why one team or contestant succeeded and the other failed, or why certain tactics worked better than others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These stories may discuss strategic changes, rule effects, practice and preparation, and historical parallels. Use analysis to interpret outcomes rather than simply recounting events (example: 'NEW RULES UPSET TEAMS' analyzing rule-change effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: General (feature) sports stories — expository surveys and trends
rubrics_metrics.description: General sports stories have small immediate news value but offer informative, significant facts, surveys, trends, or profiles about a sport suitable as feature material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topics include seasonal comparisons, profiles ('Ty Cobb's Place in Baseball History'), and trend pieces; they are valuable for Sunday editions and when athletic news is scarce.

rubrics_metrics.name: What society news covers — local, conventional social items
rubrics_metrics.description: Society news concerns local social and personal news of the paper's city/county; it is almost entirely local and deals with conventional social life, not the unconventional or abnormal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude elopements, clandestine marriages, freakish parties and other extraordinary items from the society beat; those belong in the main news columns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Society reporting — restraint, discrimination, and correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Society editing demands consistent care, discrimination and habitual restraint: recognize relative social distinctions, know what names and functions to feature, and present details acceptably to social groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extravagant praise and overblown phrasing (do not use florid boilerplate descriptions) and equally avoid trite, colorless stock phrases; maintain restraint and dignity of tone in engagements, weddings, dinners, receptions and personals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative society items — model accepted methods and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Use restrained, dignified methods for engagements, wedding announcements, dinners, dances, receptions and personals as models for society write-ups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study examples to learn acceptable phrasing, which avoids both extravagant sentimentality and dull clichés; the text shows sample engagement and wedding announcements as exemplars.
